result.summary: The text lists the kings of Alba down to Proca, then introduces Pomona, a Latin Hamadryad devoted to orchards who shuns love. Vertumnus woos her in many disguises and finally appears as an old woman who begins a speech urging her to marry him.

scenes.title: The kings of Alba
scenes.summary: The line of Alban kings is listed from Ascanius through Tiberinus and Aventinus to Proca.

scenes.title: Pomona and her orchard
scenes.summary: Pomona tends her trees, walls out the rustics, and rejects the Satyrs, Pans, Sylvanus and Priapus.
scenes.stakes: Her chosen life of gardening and freedom from love.

scenes.title: Vertumnus in disguises
scenes.summary: Vertumnus approaches Pomona as reaper, herdsman, pruner, soldier and fisherman, then as an old woman who kisses her.
scenes.stakes: Vertumnus risks yet another failed courtship.

scenes.title: The old woman's plea
scenes.summary: Using the elm and vine as an example, the disguised Vertumnus urges Pomona to marry Vertumnus and warns of the gods' anger.

notable_quotes.reason: Vertumnus disguised as an old woman kisses Pomona, a comic, revealing moment.

analysis.text: Pomona's refusal of love and Vertumnus's disguises set up a courtship about change versus self-contained devotion; the elm and vine image argues for union.
The king list gives Rome's Alban ancestry a mythic genealogy, tying Latin places like the Tiber and Aventine to legendary rulers.

legacy.text: Pomona and Vertumnus became favorite subjects of Renaissance and Baroque art, including Arcimboldo's portrait of Rudolf II as Vertumnus.

fun_facts.text: The name Pomona comes from Latin pomum, 'fruit', and the genus name Pomona is still used for fruit-related terms like pomology.

language_notes.text: Ascanius, son of Aeneas, was also called Iulus; the 'two names' refer to this. Alba Longa was the city he founded.
Tiberinus drowned in the river Albula, which was renamed the Tiber after him; Etrurian means Etruscan.
Remulus imitated Jupiter's lightning, mocking the god, and was punished by a thunderbolt.
Hamadryads are wood nymphs whose lives are bound to particular trees. Pomona's name comes from Latin pomum, 'fruit'.
Engrafting means grafting: inserting a shoot (the sucker) into a slit in the bark so it grows on another tree, the 'stranger nursling'.
'Rustics' means country people; 'flies from' means flees from, not travels by air.
The god who scares thieves is Priapus, a garden god whose statues, with a pruning-hook and exaggerated phallus, guarded orchards.
Bay-bound temples and turning mown grass describe a hay-maker, one of Vertumnus's rustic roles.
"Obtained access for himself" means he gained admission to her presence by these disguises, so he could look at her.
"Unwedded" applies marriage language to trees: vines were trained to grow up elms, a common Roman farming practice.
Helen of Troy, the Lapith bride Hippodame (whose wedding led to the battle with the Centaurs), and Penelope, wife of Ulysses, who faced her suitors, are all famous much-wooed women.
The mountains of Alba refer to Alba Longa in Latium; the Italian rural deities who live there court Pomona.
The Idalian Goddess is Venus, worshipped at Idalium in Cyprus. She of Rhamnus is Nemesis, goddess of retribution, whose shrine stood at Rhamnus in Attica.

context_notes.text: Proca is the Alban king who later fathers Numitor and Amulius, in the line leading to Romulus and Remus. The Palatine is a Roman hill.
Satyrs, Pans and Sylvanus are lustful rustic woodland spirits and gods, so they are typical pursuers of nymphs in Ovid.
Vertumnus is an Italian god of seasons and change. Pomona is a nymph devoted to orchards and fruit-growing.
The old-woman disguise lets him enter the garden and kiss Pomona, as an old woman would not be a threat in her eyes.

literary_notes.text: The pruning-knife replaces the huntress's javelin, marking Pomona as a cultivator rather than a hunter like Diana's nymphs.
A blunt statement of her delight in gardening and lack of desire defines Pomona and sets up the wooing that follows.
The question stresses how many suitors tried, building comic momentum before Vertumnus is introduced as the most persistent.
The narrator's aside emphasizes how perfectly Vertumnus plays each role, preparing the greater disguise to come.
Vertumnus's kisses are unlike any real old woman's, an ironic hint that the disguise conceals a lover.
The elm and vine stand for husband and wife; the argument from nature urges Pomona that she needs a partner.
Vertumnus, speaking as the old woman, praises his own shape-changing, which the reader knows is exactly what he has been doing.
